title: Burn Severity Shapes Post‐Fire Methane Uptake in European Boreal Forest Soils
content:
Abstract

Forest fires are increasing in frequency and severity across boreal regions, yet their long-term impact on soil methane (CH4) fluxes remains uncertain. Understanding the conditions that govern post-fire CH4 dynamics is critical for projecting fire-climate feedbacks in northern forest ecosystems. Fire severity alters soil microclimate, organic horizons, physiochemistry, and microbial function, yet severity-resolved evidence from European boreal forests remains scarce. We measured CH4 fluxes over 28 months following prescribed burns in Scots pine-dominated forests in Finland. Fire severity, quantified via field assessments and remote sensing, emerged as a key driver of post-fire CH4 uptake. Low-severity burns had greater CH4 uptake than unburned areas, resulting in an estimated 46% higher cumulative uptake over the first two growing seasons. In contrast, uptake in higher-severity burns was comparable to that in unburned areas. Maximum uptake occurred after approximately 0.3–0.4 cm of organic-horizon consumption, consistent with improved gas transport following limited removal of the surface organic layer, whereas uptake declined with greater organic-horizon consumption. Across the severity gradient, warmer and drier soils increased CH4 uptake. Hierarchical partitioning showed that soil moisture and temperature together accounted for 81.5% of the variance explained by model predictors, whereas residual organic-horizon depth and canopy mortality accounted for 17% and time since fire for 1.5%. Our findings demonstrate that post-fire CH4 uptake depends on fire severity and associated soil environmental conditions rather than on fire occurrence alone. Accounting for fire severity and soil environmental responses should improve predictions of post-fire CH4 dynamics in boreal ecosystems.
